record.narrative: No claims are available yet, so this is an initial binary-predictor screen for association with CRISPR dependency. Dependency scores are more negative when dependency is stronger. Most proposals therefore use negative direction to test whether an exposure status is associated with stronger dependency; a few use positive direction to test whether exposure status is associated with weaker/less negative dependency. For negative-direction claims, a positive signed estimate supports stronger dependency in the exposed group relative to the comparator. For positive-direction claims, a positive signed estimate supports weaker dependency in the exposed group relative to the comparator. All selected predictors are binary or near-binary numeric features with both groups represented; common-marker hypotheses expose the minority absent value where the group size is still large enough for discovery. I avoided feature_049 because it is constant, and avoided categorical variables whose minority levels could not be verified to have at least 20 observations from the supplied summary. This first wave is deliberately broad but executable, covering 12 outcomes and testing both dependency-enhancing and dependency-reducing directions. Later results will guide follow-up around outcomes with wider dispersion (for example outcome_001, outcome_006, outcome_008, outcome_011, outcome_013, outcome_014) and predictors with sufficiently large cell counts.

No evidence has yet been returned, so I will request all 12 initially registered binary main-effect analyses. This maximizes the first screen across distinct outcomes and predictors while staying within the 12-analysis limit. All comparisons appear feasible from the supplied summaries because each selected predictor has both exposed and comparator values represented with likely cell sizes above the minimum. I will assess these results in the appraise stage with emphasis on signed effect size, clinical-meaningfulness around the stated relative difference threshold, and confidence interval width rather than significance alone.

All 12 discovery comparisons were valid, with adequate cell sizes. The first-screen results are broadly null: every 95% Welch interval includes zero, and no point estimate reaches a clinically meaningful magnitude. I approximated clinical significance by a roughly 10% absolute effect on the dependency-score scale, which is about 0.025 for most outcomes given their absolute means around 0.25–0.4; for outcome_006, whose mean is near zero, I treated the relative threshold cautiously. For H1, H2, H4, H5, H9, H10, H11, and H12, the signed upper confidence bound is below the approximate clinical benchmark and/or the point estimate is small or in the opposite direction from the claimed association, so these direct main-effect hypotheses are rejected and closed for now. For H3, H6, H7, and H8, the intervals include zero but the upper bounds could plausibly exceed the clinical benchmark, so I did not fully reject them; however, the point estimates are small and unstable, so they are unresolved and deferred rather than validated. No claim is accepted. I am not requesting validation because none of these effects is large enough or sufficiently stable to justify independent confirmation over exploring additional predictors or stratified hypotheses.

No independent validation results have been delivered and there are no response deadlines for validation reassessment, so the synthesis changes are limited to the discovery evidence already assessed. The current accepted claim set remains empty. The first 12 binary comparisons were well-powered enough for Welch inference, but none showed a scientifically meaningful association: every interval includes zero, and none had a point estimate whose magnitude plus interval support crossed the 10% relative clinical threshold. Interpreting the negative dependency-score means literally, 10% relative difference corresponds roughly to an absolute shift of 0.025 for outcomes with mean magnitude near 0.25, about 0.042 for outcome_001, and a smaller absolute threshold for low-magnitude outcomes such as outcome_006 and outcome_014. For most outcomes, the confidence intervals exclude clinically meaningful effects or the point estimate is trivial/opposite to the claimed direction. The four unresolved deferred claims, H3, H6, H7, and H8, remain unresolved only because their intervals still permit effects at or near the clinical benchmark, but their point estimates are too small to support acceptance or validation. These findings are dataset-specific associations and do not establish causality or generalizability. Next, I registered 12 high-power comparisons for the previously unscreened outcomes outcome_013, outcome_014, outcome_015, and outcome_016, using the three nearly balanced binary predictors with the largest feasible cell sizes: feature_034, feature_002, and feature_060. Each direction tests whether the exposed group has stronger dependency, i.e., a more negative score; anticipated direction is uncertain because predictor labels are opaque. This focuses on outcomes that have not yet been tested and on predictors with roughly 50% prevalence, where uncertainty intervals are narrow enough to distinguish clinically meaningful effects from trivial ones.

The ledger now contains H13-H24, which already test three nearly balanced binary predictors (feature_034, feature_002, feature_060) across outcomes 013-016. To extend the same high-power strategy to outcomes where earlier binary screens were weak or where outcome scale/variance warrants tighter inference, I registered 12 additional main-effect claims: the same three balanced predictors on outcomes 001, 006, 008, and 011. feature_034 and feature_002/feature_060 have approximately half the dataset in each exposure/comparator cell, so these comparisons should have roughly 980-1040 observations per cell and therefore much narrower intervals than sparse binary comparisons. These outcomes include outcome_001, outcome_008, and outcome_011, which have wider dispersion, and outcome_006, which has a small absolute mean but large spread; all are therefore scientifically plausible targets for meaningful biological shifts. All comparisons use direction=-1, so a positive signed estimate would mean the exposed group has stronger dependency (more negative score), while a negative signed estimate would mean weaker dependency or an opposite shift. anticipated_direction=0 because predictor labels are opaque and there is no pre-evidence directional prior for feature_002 or feature_060 on these outcomes. If any balanced predictor shows a clinically meaningful effect and consistent direction across outcomes, it will be prioritized for validation; if the balanced screen is also null, the next wave should move to categorical levels, continuous threshold comparisons, or interaction/subgroup analyses only where evidence suggests heterogeneity.

There are no assessments due, so I am using the 12-analysis capacity to request the registered high-power balanced binary screen for the currently untested outcomes outcome_013, outcome_014, outcome_015, and outcome_016. These correspond to H13-H24 and test feature_034, feature_002, and feature_060 against comparator 0. All three predictors have approximately half the dataset in each cell, so discovery intervals should be substantially tighter than the sparse first-screen comparisons. This prioritizes outcomes with no prior direct evidence while maintaining scientific diversity across predictors. All claims are direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means feature=1 has stronger dependency (more negative outcome) than feature=0; a negative signed estimate would indicate weaker dependency or the opposite shift. Anticipated direction remains 0 because predictor labels are opaque. The clinical benchmark is interpreted as a relative difference of about 10% in outcome magnitude; for outcomes with mean magnitude near -0.25 to -0.27, that is roughly a 0.025 absolute dependency-score shift, with extra caution for outcome_014 because its mean is near zero but its spread is large. If any of H13-H24 produces a clinically sized point estimate or an interval that strongly excludes trivial effects, the next stage should prioritize follow-up or validation. If all 12 are small/null, I would close this outcome-predictor block as high-power but uninformative and move to H25-H36 for high-dispersion outcomes 001, 006, 008, and 011.

All 12 new balanced-predictor comparisons are valid and have large cell sizes, so the main scientific issue is not feasibility but whether the signed effect sizes and uncertainty intervals support a clinically meaningful association. For these direction -1 claims, a positive signed estimate means feature=1 has a more negative dependency score than feature=0, i.e., stronger dependency; a negative signed estimate means the opposite, weaker dependency. I used approximately 10% of the absolute outcome mean as the clinical benchmark: about 0.025 for outcome_013, 0.015, and 0.016, and about 0.009 for outcome_014, with extra caution for outcome_014 because its mean is near zero and a relative threshold is unstable there.

H13 (outcome_013/feature_034) has a signed estimate of -0.0187, indicating the opposite of the claimed stronger-dependency direction. Its signed upper bound, 0.0012, is far below the clinical benchmark, so clinically meaningful stronger dependency is ruled out; H13 is rejected and closed. The same evidence suggests a possible weaker-dependency signal, so I registered a direction +1 refinement rather than accepting H13. H14 (outcome_013/feature_002) has a tiny positive estimate and an upper bound 0.0235 below the approximate benchmark, so I rejected it. H15 (outcome_013/feature_060) is not robustly positive, but its upper bound 0.0328 exceeds the benchmark; it is unresolved and deferred.

For outcome_014, H16-H18 all have near-zero point estimates and wide intervals. Because outcome_014's mean is close to zero, the 10% relative benchmark is numerically small and can be unstable; therefore I did not reject these solely because the point estimates are small, but I also did not accept them. They remain unresolved and deferred.

For outcome_015, H20 and H21 have small effects and upper confidence bounds well below the benchmark, so they are rejected and closed. H19 (outcome_015/feature_034) is the only new result whose interval entirely excludes zero: signed estimate 0.0170, interval [0.0017, 0.0323]. This supports stronger dependency for feature_034=1, but the point estimate is below the approximate 10% benchmark and the interval straddles the threshold. It is scientifically interesting but not sufficient for acceptance. I marked H19 active and request validation to assess whether the effect is stable and whether it might be clinically meaningful. H20 and H21 do not receive validation.

For outcome_016, H23 has a small negative point estimate and upper bound below the benchmark, so it is rejected. H22 and H24 also have signed upper bounds below the benchmark for the claimed stronger-dependency direction, so those original claims are rejected and closed. However, their lower signed bounds indicate the raw effect is on the opposite side, suggesting possible weaker-dependency associations. I registered direction +1 refinements for H22/feature_034 and H24/feature_060 to evaluate that opposite hypothesis cleanly. No claim is accepted based solely on these discovery results, and these are associations in this dataset only, not causal or generalizable effects.

The independent validation for H19 (outcome_015 with feature_034=1 versus 0, direction -1) does not support the discovery signal and therefore leads me to reject H19. For direction -1, a positive signed estimate means the exposed group has stronger dependency, i.e., a more negative outcome_015 score. The discovery estimate was +0.0170 (95% interval +0.0017 to +0.0323). Although it excluded zero, its point estimate was below the approximately 10% absolute clinical benchmark for outcome_015, about 0.025, and its interval straddled that benchmark. The independent validation estimate was in the opposite direction, -0.0046, with a very wide independent interval from -0.0277 to +0.0185. Even the signed validation upper bound, +0.0185, is below the clinically meaningful stronger-dependency benchmark, and the point estimate is negative, indicating weaker rather than stronger dependency. The combined evidence is therefore inconsistent, not clinically large enough, and insufficient to accept a scientifically meaningful association between feature_034 and outcome_015 in this dataset. I close this investigation.

At this point the accepted claim set remains empty. The overall pattern across the binary screen is broadly null or unstable: most comparisons have small signed point estimates, intervals that include zero, and no robust effect reaching the 10% relative benchmark. Several findings remain unresolved and deferred because their confidence intervals still permit clinically meaningful effects despite weak point estimates: H3, H6, H7, and H8 from the first screen, plus H15-H18 for the balanced-predictor outcomes. The opposite-direction refinements H37, H38, and H39 are scientifically plausible because they correspond to weak or reverse dependencies suggested by earlier discovery intervals, but they are near the clinical threshold and lack replication. They should not be validated before the currently registered high-power H25-H36 screen is completed. The next most informative analysis is to run H25-H36, testing feature_034, feature_002, and feature_060 on outcomes 001, 006, 008, and 011. These outcomes include high-dispersion and low-magnitude outcomes, and the balanced predictors provide approximately 1000 observations per cell. If that screen is also null, I would close this binary main-effect strategy and pivot to categorical predictor contrasts or interaction/subgroup analyses only where near-threshold evidence supports conditional effects. All conclusions so far are dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

There are no assessments due at this stage, so I am registering a new wave of scientifically motivated interaction hypotheses rather than repeating existing main-effect claims. The accumulated evidence is dominated by small marginal binary contrasts, including a validation failure for the strongest discovery signal, H19. One plausible explanation is that additive main-effect comparisons mask context-specific combinatorial effects: a dependency-relevant cell-state pattern may show stronger effect when two balanced labels co-occur, while averaging over the other level dilutes the marginal association. Therefore I registered 12 interaction contrasts among the three nearly balanced predictors feature_002, feature_034, and feature_060. These predictors provide approximately 250 observations per cell in a 2x2 interaction design, so the analyses should be well-powered relative to sparse binary comparisons.

Each new proposal uses direction -1. For direction -1, a positive signed interaction estimate corresponds to the exposure having a more negative effect, i.e., stronger CRISPR dependency, in the subgroup defined by the second balanced predictor than in the complement subgroup. A negative signed estimate would suggest antagonism or weaker dependency in that context, and an interval including zero would support null or conditional ambiguity. anticipated_direction=0 because predictor labels are opaque and I do not have a pre-specified directional prior for interactions among these labels. Plausible alternatives include no interaction, a clinically meaningful positive interaction, or a negative interaction of comparable magnitude.

I restricted this interaction screen to outcomes with reasonably stable absolute dependency-score means and scientifically interpretable 10% thresholds: outcome_011, outcome_013, outcome_015, and outcome_016. The approximate absolute clinical benchmarks are about 0.030 for outcome_011, 0.027 for outcome_013, 0.025 for outcome_015, and 0.026 for outcome_016. I deliberately avoided interactions on outcome_006 and outcome_014 for now because their means are close to zero, making a 10% relative threshold unstable and potentially requiring a different absolute-scale scientific judgment. These proposals are associations only; they do not assume causality or generalizability beyond the supplied dataset.

For the immediate next analysis step, the highest-priority registered claims should remain H25-H36, the high-power balanced main-effect screen on outcomes 001, 006, 008, and 011. The newly registered interaction claims are queued for follow-up, especially if the pending main-effect screen remains null or if existing near-threshold reverse refinements H37-H39 appear to represent biologically coherent but context-dependent patterns.

There are no assessments due, so the analysis capacity is best used to request the registered high-power main-effect screen H25-H36. These 12 claims test feature_034, feature_002, and feature_060 against comparator 0 for outcomes outcome_001, outcome_006, outcome_008, and outcome_011. Each predictor is nearly balanced, so the discovery Welch analyses should have roughly 980-1040 observations per cell and therefore much sharper uncertainty intervals than the earlier sparse binary screens. I am prioritizing these over the newly registered interaction claims because interactions require four cells and are lower-powered; the marginal screen first establishes whether these broadly distributed labels are associated with any clinically meaningful shift in dependency. All selected claims use direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means feature=1 has a more negative dependency score than feature=0, i.e., stronger dependency. The 10% relative clinical benchmark corresponds approximately to 0.042 for outcome_001, 0.009 for outcome_006, 0.028 for outcome_008, and 0.030 for outcome_011; outcome_006 will need extra caution because its mean is close to zero and the relative threshold is numerically unstable. If these main effects are broadly null, the interaction claims remain useful but will need to be interpreted cautiously and will likely close the balanced binary main-effect strategy unless a strong near-threshold reverse or interaction signal emerges.

All 12 new high-power balanced-predictor discoveries are valid. For these direction -1 claims, a positive signed estimate means feature=1 has stronger dependency (more negative outcome) than feature=0, while a negative signed estimate means the opposite. I evaluated them using the approximately 10% absolute-mean benchmark: about 0.042 for outcome_001, 0.009 for outcome_006, 0.028 for outcome_008, and 0.030 for outcome_011, with explicit caution for outcome_006 because its mean is near zero and the relative threshold is numerically unstable. H25 and H26 have small positive point estimates and upper bounds below the outcome_001 benchmark, so clinically meaningful stronger dependency is ruled out; both are rejected and closed. H27 remains unresolved because its upper bound exceeds the benchmark, although the point estimate is far below it. For outcome_006, H28 and H29 are not clinically supported by point estimates, but their upper bounds exceed the unstable 10% benchmark, so they are unresolved and deferred rather than rejected. H30 is the only new candidate whose point estimate exceeds that benchmark (+0.0235), but its 95% interval includes zero and the outcome mean is near zero, making the relative clinical criterion unstable; I leave it unresolved and active as a possible follow-up signal but do not consider it acceptable. For outcome_008, H33 is rejected and closed because its upper bound (+0.0280) is below the benchmark (+0.0282); H31 and H32 remain unresolved because their upper bounds exceed the benchmark even though point estimates do not. For outcome_011, H35 and H36 are rejected and closed for the claimed stronger-dependency direction because their signed upper bounds are far below the benchmark, and both point estimates are negative. H34 remains unresolved because its upper bound exceeds the benchmark. Overall, this high-power main-effect screen is mostly null: no interval robustly supports a clinically meaningful stronger-dependency association. I am not requesting validation for H30 because the independent validation interval would be very conservative and H30 is not robust in discovery, especially with an unstable relative benchmark on near-zero outcome_006. The next priority is the already registered interaction screen H40-H51, which can reveal context-specific effects that marginal main effects may mask. I also registered a reverse-direction refinement for outcome_011/feature_002 because H35's raw negative estimate suggests the opposite association (weaker dependency) as a separate scientific hypothesis. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable effects.

The newly released independent validation for H13 resolves the original stronger-dependency hypothesis for outcome_013 with feature_034. H13 uses direction -1, so a positive signed estimate would mean feature_034=1 is associated with a more negative, i.e., stronger, CRISPR dependency score than feature_034=0. The discovery signed estimate was -0.0187 (95% Welch interval -0.0385 to +0.0012), opposite to the claimed stronger-dependency direction, and its upper bound was far below the approximately 10% absolute clinical benchmark for outcome_013, about 0.0269. The independent validation estimate was also negative for H13, -0.0053, with a conservative independent interval from -0.0348 to +0.0241. The validation upper bound is below the 10% benchmark, so clinically meaningful stronger dependency for feature_034=1 is not supported and can be ruled out. I therefore reject H13 and close that marginal stronger-dependency investigation.

The same evidence applies to the reverse refinement H37, outcome_013 feature_034 direction +1, where a positive signed estimate means feature_034=1 is associated with weaker dependency. H37 has signed estimates +0.0187 in discovery and +0.0053 in independent validation. The discovery interval included zero and crossed the clinical threshold, while the validation interval was wide, crossed zero, and had a point estimate far below the threshold. I do not accept H37 because the point estimates are not clinically meaningful and validation does not replicate a threshold-level effect. However, because the validation upper bound still permits a clinically meaningful weaker-dependency effect, I retain it as unresolved but deferred rather than formally rejecting it. The same logic applies to other near-threshold reverse or weak main-effect claims: H38, H39, and H52 have intervals that can still permit clinical effects in one direction, but their point estimates are weak and unvalidated, so they are deferred rather than treated as active priorities. H30 is also deferred: its point estimate exceeded the unstable outcome_006 threshold, but its interval included zero and outcome_006 has a near-zero mean, making the 10% relative benchmark scientifically unstable.

The accepted claim set remains empty. The accumulated evidence across binary and balanced-predictor marginal screens is broadly null or inconsistent. H19 was rejected after its independent validation reversed direction and was not clinically meaningful. H13 is now also rejected and closed after validation ruled out clinically meaningful stronger dependency. Many rejected claims have upper bounds below the clinical benchmark, while a larger number remain unresolved because intervals still allow effects at or above 10%, especially for H3, H6, H7, H8, H15-H18, H27-H34, H37-H39, and H52. None of these have sufficient evidence to support acceptance. The most informative next step is to complete the registered interaction screen H40-H51 among the three nearly balanced predictors feature_002, feature_034, and feature_060 for outcomes with stable absolute thresholds: outcome_011, outcome_013, outcome_015, and outcome_016. These tests can reveal context-specific associations that marginal main effects may mask. If the interaction screen is also null, I would close the balanced binary strategy and pivot to multi-level categorical contrasts or carefully defined numeric/subgroup hypotheses, while still treating all associations as dataset-specific rather than causal or generalizable.

The accepted set is still empty, and the evidence so far suggests that the three nearly balanced binary predictors feature_002, feature_034, and feature_060 do not have robust marginal effects. The next logical step is to widen the predictor screen in a way that remains analytically powerful and clinically interpretable. I registered one reverse-direction claim for feature_037 on outcome_011 because the prior claim H11 tested the opposite direction and showed a raw exposed-minus-comparator estimate near -0.022, which under direction -1 corresponds to a signed estimate of about +0.022 with an interval still wide enough to include the approximate 10% absolute-mean clinical threshold for outcome_011, about 0.030. This is a focused follow-up after a rejected marginal hypothesis, not a confirmation of the rejected claim.

I also registered main-effect tests for several previously untested binary predictors with prevalence around 0.19-0.26: feature_045, feature_021, feature_012, feature_027, and feature_050. These have roughly 375-510 exposed and 1500+ comparator observations, so Welch comparisons should have reasonably tight discovery intervals compared with sparse binary features. I placed them on outcome_011 and outcome_015 because both have stable negative means and therefore meaningful 10% absolute thresholds, about 0.030 and 0.025 respectively, without the severe instability of comparisons on outcomes with means very near zero. All main-effect claims use direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed level has a more negative dependency score, i.e., stronger CRISPR dependency, than the comparator level.

Finally, I registered a robust two-level categorical contrast for feature_054, comparing the minority level level_002 against the majority level level_001 for outcome_013. Feature_054 has a large minority group, about 578 observations if level_001 contains the 1422 majority cases, giving a well-powered comparison against the outcome_013 10% threshold of roughly 0.027. This expands the screen beyond the already saturated feature_002/feature_034/feature_060 binary family while avoiding very rare categorical levels that might fail the minimum-cell-size requirement. The highest-priority pending analyses should still be the registered interactions H40-H51; if those interactions are broadly null, the newly registered moderate-prevalence main effects provide the next informative broad screen. All proposals remain associations in this dataset and do not imply causality or generalizability.

There are no assessments due at this stage. The most informative pending analyses are the registered 12 interaction contrasts, H40-H51. These test whether associations among the three nearly balanced binary predictors feature_002, feature_034, and feature_060 differ across the complementary subgroup levels on outcomes with relatively stable absolute dependency-score means: outcome_013, outcome_015, outcome_016, and outcome_011. This complements the now mostly null or inconsistent marginal main-effect screens and can identify context-specific combinatorial associations that additive comparisons may miss. All are direction -1 claims, so a positive signed interaction estimate means the exposed contrast has a more negative dependency score, i.e., stronger dependency, within the named subgroup than in the complement subgroup. These analyses are lower-powered than marginal screens because they use four cells, but the balanced predictors make the cell sizes feasible. If these interactions are broadly null, the balanced-binary interaction strategy can be closed or down-weighted, allowing a pivot to multi-level categorical contrasts or carefully specified numeric contrasts.

These are direction -1 interaction claims, so a positive signed estimate means the contrast within the named subgroup is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e., stronger CRISPR dependency, than the contrast in the subgroup complement. I applied the 10% relative benchmark using each outcome's approximate absolute mean: about 0.0269 for outcome_013, 0.0250 for outcome_015, 0.0256 for outcome_016, and 0.0301 for outcome_011. H43 and H47 are rejected for the claimed stronger-dependency direction because their upper confidence bounds are below the relevant threshold: H43 upper 0.0173 < 0.0250 and H47 upper 0.0128 < 0.0256. H40, H41, H42, H44, H45, H46, H48, H49, and H50 are not accepted because their point estimates are below the clinical benchmark, several are in the opposite direction, and their intervals are too imprecise; I leave them unresolved and deferred. H51 is the only candidate with a clinically suggestive point estimate: outcome_011 feature_060 interaction within feature_002=1 is +0.0409, above the 0.0301 threshold, with a 95% interval from -0.0052 to +0.0870. Because the interval crosses zero and the interaction screen had 12 comparisons, this is not yet evidence supporting acceptance. It is, however, the best available candidate for follow-up, so I request independent validation of H51. The accepted set remains empty.

I reassessed H19 because its scheduled independent validation response has arrived, and I assessed the newly delivered validation for H51. For H19, the claim is outcome_015 with feature_034=1 versus feature_034=0 under direction -1, so a positive signed estimate would indicate stronger CRISPR dependency in the exposed group. The approximately 10% absolute clinical benchmark for outcome_015 is about 0.0250. The discovery signed estimate was +0.0170, below the clinical benchmark, although its lower bound was positive and its upper bound permitted a clinically meaningful effect. The independent validation estimate was opposite to the claimed direction, -0.0046, with a conservative independent interval from -0.0277 to +0.0185. The validation point estimate is essentially null and its upper bound is below the 0.0250 benchmark, so clinically meaningful stronger dependency for feature_034=1 on outcome_015 is not supported. This resolves H19 as a negative finding, and I reject and close it. For H51, the claim is the interaction of feature_060 within feature_002=1 for outcome_011, also direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means the feature_060 contrast is associated with stronger dependency inside the feature_002=1 subgroup than in the complement subgroup. The clinical benchmark for outcome_011 is about 0.0301. The discovery estimate was +0.0409 with a 95% interval from -0.0052 to +0.0870, and the independent validation estimate was +0.0314 with a very wide independent interval from -0.0376 to +0.1004. Both point estimates are consistent in the claimed direction and nominally above the clinical benchmark, which makes H51 the most promising remaining candidate. However, the discovery interval includes zero, the validation interval is very imprecise and includes zero, and the claim was selected from a 12-interaction screen. The evidence therefore does not robustly support acceptance of a clinically meaningful interaction at this time. It is also not appropriate to reject H51 because the independent point estimate remains threshold-level and the upper bound permits a clinically meaningful effect. I therefore keep H51 unresolved and active. Overall, the accepted set remains empty. The supported scientific conclusion from completed work is that most tested binary marginal associations, and especially feature_034 on outcome_015, do not show clinically meaningful stronger dependency associations after independent validation. Negative findings include H19, along with many earlier binary contrasts whose confidence bounds ruled out the 10% benchmark. Unresolved uncertainty remains concentrated in context-specific interaction signals, especially H51, and in several near-threshold claims whose intervals remain wide. The most informative next analysis is to decompose H51 using direct subgroup mean differences: test feature_060=1 versus 0 separately when feature_002=1 and when feature_002=0. This will determine whether the apparent interaction reflects a clinically meaningful subgroup effect, a null complement effect, or noise. These direct contrasts should be followed alongside the pending moderate-prevalence main-effect screen and categorical contrast. If the direct contrasts do not show threshold-level subgroup evidence, the balanced-binary interaction strategy should be closed. If they show a clear subgroup-specific association, a refined direct claim can be assessed. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal effects or generalizable claims.

There are no assessments due. The accepted set remains empty, and H51 remains the strongest but unproven context-specific candidate. Its registered direct decompositions H65 and H66 should still be analyzed first because they determine whether the H51 interaction reflects a clinically meaningful feature_060 effect in the feature_002=1 subgroup, a weak/null complement effect, or noise.

To avoid leaving other plausible interaction candidates in an ambiguous unresolved state, I registered direct mean-difference decompositions for the two next-best outcome_011 interaction claims, H49 and H50. H49 tested feature_002-by-feature_034 and H50 tested feature_060-by-feature_034. Both have positive signed estimates below the approximate 10% absolute-mean threshold for outcome_011, about 0.0301, and wide intervals. Direct contrasts within feature_034=1 versus feature_034=0 will clarify whether either predictor has a subgroup-specific association large enough to matter clinically. These are direction -1 claims, so positive signed estimates mean the exposed level is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency, within the subgroup. I anticipated a negative raw contrast in feature_034=1 for the exposures whose parent interactions were nominally positive, and no direction for the complements because the interaction alone cannot determine whether the complement is null or opposite.

I also registered follow-up main-effect tests for feature_037, whose outcome_011 candidate H53 has signed estimate +0.0221 with 95% interval -0.0086 to +0.0528. That is below the outcome_011 clinical benchmark but still compatible with a clinically meaningful stronger-dependency effect. Rather than multiply hypotheses on the same outcome, I tested feature_037 across the relatively stable negative-scale outcomes outcome_015, outcome_013, and outcome_016, with absolute 10% thresholds approximately 0.0250, 0.0269, and 0.0256. A repeated threshold-level or interval-supported effect would strengthen the case for a real dataset association; null or threshold-excluded results across these outcomes would support closing feature_037 as a main-effect candidate.

Finally, I registered feature_054 level_002 versus level_001 main effects for outcome_011, outcome_015, and outcome_016. This complements the already pending feature_054/outcome_013 claim H64. Feature_054 is a binary categorical predictor with a large minority level, so comparisons should be feasible and more stable than sparse binary screens. The levels are opaque nominal labels, so I did not impose an expected direction. These proposals expand the robust categorical screen beyond the balanced binary family while avoiding outcomes whose absolute means are very near zero and whose 10% relative benchmark is scientifically unstable or imprecise.

The next analysis priority should be the direct H51 decompositions H65 and H66, then the pending moderate-prevalence binary main effects H54-H63 and the robust categorical H64. Newly registered direct decompositions and follow-up screens are useful, but if analysis capacity is limited, H65 and H66 should not be displaced because they most directly resolve the only clinically suggestive interaction candidate. All claims remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable effects.

No assessments are due. I selected 12 claims to maximize the immediate information gain while staying within the analysis limit. The highest-priority claims are H65 and H66, the direct mean-difference decompositions of the only clinically suggestive interaction candidate, H51. H65 tests feature_060=1 versus 0 within feature_002=1, and H66 tests the complement feature_002=0. Because these are direction -1 claims, a positive signed estimate means stronger CRISPR dependency in the exposed level. These direct contrasts will show whether the apparent interaction in H51 reflects a subgroup-specific association, a broad main effect, or noise.

The remaining analyses extend the robust moderate-prevalence binary screen. I prioritized feature_045, feature_021, feature_012, and feature_027 on both outcome_011 and outcome_015, where they have reasonably large exposed and comparator cells. I prioritized feature_050 on outcome_015 over outcome_011 because outcome_015 has a lower absolute mean threshold and smaller outcome SD, giving a more detectable contrast. I also included H64, the feature_054 level_002 versus level_001 contrast for outcome_013, because it adds a robust categorical predictor and has large enough cells to evaluate the approximate 10% absolute-mean benchmark. I deferred feature_050 on outcome_011, the feature_037 and feature_054 follow-up outcomes, and the additional direct decompositions of lower-priority interaction claims for later iterations. These requested comparisons remain dataset-specific associations; positive results will be judged against the approximate clinical benchmarks and then considered for validation if sufficiently compelling.

All newly delivered claims were direction -1 tests, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed level is associated with a more negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency. I applied the approximate clinical benchmark as 10% of the absolute outcome mean: about 0.0301 for outcome_011, 0.0250 for outcome_015, and 0.0269 for outcome_013. The direct decomposition of H51 does not support a clinically meaningful stronger-dependency effect in the feature_002=1 subgroup: H65 is only +0.0136, below the outcome_011 benchmark, with an interval that both includes zero and crosses the benchmark. H66, the complementary feature_002=0 subgroup, has a signed estimate of -0.0273, opposite the claimed stronger-dependency direction, with upper bound far below the benchmark; I reject H66 for the claimed direction. Taken together, H51 appears to be an interaction between two imprecise sub-threshold contrasts, not evidence of a clinically meaningful feature_060 effect in the feature_002=1 subgroup. Since H51 has already been independently validated with a very wide interval, I keep it unresolved but defer it rather than pursue it further now. Among the moderate-prevalence binary screens, H54, H56, H57, H58, and H59 are rejected for the claimed stronger-dependency direction because their upper bounds are below the relevant 10% benchmark, often with point estimates in the opposite direction. H55, H60, H61, H63, and H64 remain unresolved because their point estimates are below the clinical benchmark but their upper bounds permit a clinically meaningful effect; however, none is strong enough to justify immediate validation or acceptance. No new acceptance is supported, and I request no additional validation because the new results do not establish threshold-level evidence and the best interaction candidate, H51, is already validated but remains imprecise and uninformative after direct decomposition.

H13 is the claim that outcome_013 dependency is stronger for feature_034=1 versus feature_034=0 under direction -1; thus a positive signed estimate would indicate stronger dependency in the exposed group. The clinically meaningful absolute benchmark is approximately 0.0269, using the outcome_013 mean of about -0.269. The discovery estimate was opposite the claimed direction, -0.0187, with 95% interval -0.0385 to +0.0012. The independent validation estimate was also opposite, -0.0053, with independent interval -0.0348 to +0.0241. The validation upper bound is below the 10% benchmark, so the evidence does not support a clinically meaningful stronger-dependency association for feature_034 on outcome_013. I therefore keep H13 rejected and closed, now including the validation evidence in the assessment.

The broader state after this iteration is that the accepted set remains empty. The most interpretable negative findings are that tested binary marginal contrasts do not show clinically meaningful stronger-dependency effects once intervals are compared with outcome-specific 10%-of-absolute-mean benchmarks. Examples include feature_034 on outcome_015 and outcome_013, many moderate-prevalence binary contrasts on outcome_011 and outcome_015, and complementary subgroups that were either opposite or too small in magnitude. For outcome_011, the approximate benchmark is 0.0301; H65, the direct feature_060 effect within feature_002=1, is only +0.0136 with interval -0.0186 to +0.0458, while H66 in the feature_002=0 subgroup is -0.0273 with interval -0.0603 to +0.0057. These direct decompositions do not support a clinically meaningful feature_060 subgroup effect and weaken H51, even though H51 remains technically unresolved because both original and validated interaction intervals remain wide.

Unresolved uncertainty is now concentrated in near-threshold but imprecise candidates: feature_037 on outcome_011, H37 as the reversed feature_034 direction on outcome_013, H65/H51 interactions, and several upper bounds that permit threshold-level effects despite subthreshold point estimates. These are not accepted and should not be treated as evidence of generalizable or causal associations. The most informative next analysis is to stop expanding the balanced-binary interaction family and instead complete the pending robust main-effect screens for feature_050, feature_037, and feature_054 across outcome_011, outcome_013, outcome_015, and outcome_016, while adding two diverse robust categorical screens, feature_063 and feature_019. A new candidate would merit acceptance or validation only if its point estimate is at or above the outcome-specific 10% benchmark and its interval is no longer compatible with a null or below-threshold contrast.

There are no assessments due, and the accepted set remains empty. Prior evidence does not support a clinically meaningful balanced-binary interaction family: H51 remains technically unresolved, but its direct decompositions H65 and H66 are sub-threshold and inconsistent, so I will not continue adding similar interactions unless a direct subgroup contrast becomes compelling. The most productive next comparisons are therefore robust main-effect screens with adequate cell sizes, using stable negative-scale outcomes rather than outcomes whose absolute means are near zero and make the 10% clinical threshold hard to interpret.

All new proposals use direction -1. For these direction -1 claims, a positive signed estimate means the exposed level is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency, relative to the comparator. I am using an approximate clinical magnitude benchmark equal to 10% of the absolute outcome mean: about 0.0250 for outcome_015, 0.0256 for outcome_016, 0.0269 for outcome_013, and 0.0282 for outcome_008. The new tests are intentionally falsifiable: if the point estimate is below the benchmark and the confidence interval upper bound is also below it, I will reject that predictor-outcome contrast for the claimed stronger-dependency direction; if the point estimate is at or above the benchmark and the interval excludes both null and clinically small effects, the claim becomes an acceptance or validation candidate; if the interval remains wide and crosses the benchmark or zero, the claim stays unresolved but low priority.

I propose feature_042 and feature_065 because both have adequate exposed counts and have not yet been tested on the high-power outcomes outcome_015, outcome_016, and outcome_013. I propose feature_030 and feature_064 as high-prevalence binary screens on outcome_015, with the low level as exposed; these are not sparse enough to fall below the 20-per-cell requirement, but their minority cells are smaller, so they are most informative if the observed contrast is near or above threshold. I propose feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 because feature_055 is a robust categorical predictor: its top level has 519 observations and, given four levels with largest frequency 519, every level should be large enough for a stable comparison. This adds an opaque categorical predictor without relying on small levels. I also propose feature_037 on outcome_008 as a consistency check for the near-threshold feature_037 signal on outcome_011. I anticipated a raw negative contrast on outcome_008 only because the earlier outcome_011 candidate favored stronger dependency in feature_037=1; otherwise categorical labels have no inherent direction. Finally, feature_005 on outcome_015 adds one untested moderate-prevalence binary screen on the outcome with the lowest clinically meaningful magnitude benchmark.

These claims remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable effects. If analysis capacity is limited, I would prioritize the already registered robust categorical and near-threshold main-effect screens (feature_037, feature_050, feature_054, feature_063, feature_019) together with the new feature_055, feature_042, and feature_065 comparisons, because they are more likely to provide interpretable acceptance, rejection, or deferral decisions than further broadening the interaction space.

No assessments are due. I selected 12 registered but unanalyzed main-effect claims because the current evidence is concentrated on near-threshold, imprecise robust predictors, whereas further balanced-binary interaction exploration appears low-yield after H51 and its direct decompositions H65/H66. All selected claims use direction -1 mean differences: a positive signed estimate indicates a more negative dependency score in the exposed group, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. I am judging new candidates against approximate outcome-specific 10%-of-absolute-mean benchmarks, about 0.0301 for outcome_011, 0.0250 for outcome_015, 0.0269 for outcome_013, and 0.0256 for outcome_016.

H62 completes the feature_050 main-effect screen on outcome_011 after outcome_015 was already tested; feature_050 has adequate exposed and comparator cells and is a reasonable moderate-prevalence binary predictor. H71 through H73 test feature_037 on outcome_015, outcome_013, and outcome_016, giving cross-outcome consistency for the near-threshold feature_037 candidate originally seen on outcome_011. H74 through H76 test feature_054 level_002 versus level_001 on outcome_011, outcome_015, and outcome_016, completing a robust binary categorical screen for which outcome_013 was already tested. H77 through H79 add robust categorical screens on feature_063 and feature_019 across lower-variance or moderately negative-scale outcomes. Finally, H86 and H87 test feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_015 and outcome_016; feature_055 has a large top level, so this adds another reasonably powered categorical comparison while avoiding sparse levels.

I deferred further direct interaction decompositions and lower-priority sparse/high-prevalence screens because the most informative next evidence is whether any robust main-effect predictor repeatedly reaches or exceeds the clinical benchmark with intervals excluding both null and below-threshold contrasts. These analyses remain dataset-specific association tests; acceptance or validation would require a stronger threshold-supported effect than the current near-threshold candidates.

All due analyses were direction -1 mean differences, so a positive signed estimate indicates that the exposed level is associated with a more negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency, relative to the comparator. I compared signed upper bounds with approximate outcome-specific 10%-of-absolute-mean benchmarks: about 0.0301 for outcome_011, 0.0250 for outcome_015, 0.0269 for outcome_013, and 0.0256 for outcome_016. I did not adjust formally for multiplicity, but because many screens have now been run, I required more than a marginal upper-bound crossing before considering a result clinically meaningful.

H62, feature_050=1 versus 0 on outcome_011, is not clinically supported as a stronger-dependency association: the signed estimate is only +0.0033, close to null, and the interval crosses zero. Its upper bound is only about 0.0023 above the benchmark, so I keep the claim unresolved only because the confidence bound technically permits a threshold-level effect, but I defer it as low priority. H86, feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_015, is the most interesting new candidate: +0.0211 with interval -0.0005 to +0.0428. The point estimate is below the 0.0250 benchmark and the interval includes zero, so it does not support acceptance now. It remains active because it is near threshold and feature_055 is a reasonably powered categorical comparison, but I do not request validation yet: the current discovery evidence is not threshold-supported, and H87 for the same contrast on outcome_016 is already below threshold. Validation is more justified if feature_055 also shows a threshold-level or near-threshold signal on outcome_013 or the newly registered outcome_011 comparison.

The feature_037 follow-ups H71 through H73 are inconsistent with the earlier unresolved outcome_011 candidate. On outcome_015 the estimate is -0.0048, on outcome_013 it is -0.0010, and on outcome_016 it is -0.0092; in all three, the upper bound is well below the relevant benchmark and often the point estimate is in the opposite direction. I therefore reject these direction -1 claims for clinically meaningful stronger dependency and close them. This replication failure lowers priority for H53, although I keep H53 technically unresolved because its outcome_011 interval still crosses the benchmark.

The feature_054 screens H74 through H76 are all rejected for the claimed direction: their point estimates are near null or opposite the claimed stronger-dependency direction, and their upper bounds are below the relevant clinical benchmarks. Similarly, feature_063 on outcome_015 and outcome_013, H77 and H78, have point estimates well below threshold with upper bounds below the benchmarks, and feature_019 on outcome_016, H79, has an opposite-signed point estimate with an upper bound far below threshold. These are closed negative findings for the specified comparison. H87, feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_016, is also rejected because its upper bound is near the null and far below the benchmark.

Overall, no new acceptance is supported. The new evidence strengthens the conclusion that most tested binary and robust categorical marginal contrasts in this dataset do not show clinically meaningful stronger-dependency associations once the 10% benchmark and uncertainty are considered. I also deferred H53 and the feature_034-subgroup direct contrasts H67 through H70 because current feature_034 evidence is negative or uninformative, and adding more marginal subgroup or interaction screens appears low-yield compared with completing the feature_055, feature_042, feature_065, and other registered robust main-effect screens.

New validation and response deadlines were assessed with the same outcome-specific clinical benchmark of roughly 10 percent of absolute mean and conservative interpretation of interval uncertainty. For direction -1 claims, a positive signed estimate means the exposed contrast is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. H51 is a feature_060-by-feature_002 interaction on outcome_011, whose benchmark is about 0.0301. The discovery signed interaction estimate was +0.0409, but the 95 percent interval crossed zero, and the independent validation signed estimate was +0.0314 with a very wide independent interval from -0.0376 to +0.1004. The validation point is only about at the benchmark and the interval is compatible with no effect, a below-threshold effect, or a much larger effect. Direct decomposition is also uninformative: H65, the feature_060 effect within feature_002=1, is only +0.0136, while H66 in the complementary feature_002=0 subgroup is -0.0273, opposite the claimed direction. I therefore do not accept H51. I keep its status unresolved because the wide validated interaction point cannot fully exclude clinically meaningful heterogeneity, but I close it as a low-priority investigation because independent validation did not sharpen it and the component effects are not threshold-level. H33 is feature_060=1 versus 0 on outcome_008 under direction -1, with benchmark about 0.0282. The discovery estimate was +0.0064 with upper bound +0.0280, already below the benchmark. The new validation estimate was -0.0032 and the multiplicity-adjusted interval was -0.0347 to +0.0283; the upper bound only barely touches the benchmark and the point estimate is near zero or opposite direction. This does not support a clinically meaningful stronger-dependency association, so I reject and close H33 with both discovery and validation evidence. Overall, the accepted set remains empty. The evidence base supports several negative dataset-specific findings: feature_034 on outcome_013 and outcome_015, feature_060 on outcome_008 and outcome_016, feature_037 on outcome_015, outcome_013, and outcome_016, and feature_054 and feature_063 on screened outcomes are not clinically meaningful stronger-dependency associations for the tested directions. Unresolved uncertainty is limited to near-threshold or imprecise candidates such as H51, H86, H53, H65, and reversed feature_034 contrasts; these are not accepted and should not be treated as causal or generalizable. The most informative next analysis is to complete the already registered robust main-effect screens, prioritizing feature_055 across outcome_013 and outcome_011 via H88 and H91, then feature_042, feature_065, feature_030, feature_064, feature_005, and feature_037 on outcome_008. I would request validation for a new candidate only if its point estimate is at or above the outcome-specific benchmark with an interval that excludes null and clinically small effects, or if multiple correlated outcomes give a consistent threshold-level pattern.

No assessments are currently due, and the accepted set remains empty. The best supported but unaccepted candidate is feature_055: H86 compares level_003 with level_001 on outcome_015 and has a near-threshold positive signed estimate, +0.0211, with an interval that includes zero and below-threshold effects relative to the outcome_015 benchmark of about 0.0250. H87 for the same feature_055 contrast on outcome_016 is already not clinically meaningful, so I am now using follow-up to determine whether H86 is a robust feature_055 signal or a level-specific/level_001-specific artifact.

For all new direction -1 mean differences, a positive signed estimate means the exposed level is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency, than the comparator. I propose level_002 versus level_001 and level_003 versus level_002 on outcome_015 as a comparator audit. If level_003 is genuinely associated with stronger dependency, the signal should either follow a coherent pattern relative to level_001 or be especially clear in level_003 versus level_002. If all contrasts remain near null, I will reject or defer the feature_055 family rather than pursue validation. I also register level_002 versus level_001 on outcome_013 and outcome_011, and level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_008, to test cross-outcome consistency while the already active level_003-versus-level_001 outcome_013 and outcome_011 claims complete.

Finally, I propose feature_063 level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_015 as a focused categorical follow-up because the previous feature_063 level_002-versus-level_001 comparison on outcome_015 was null. The third level may be biologically distinct, but if it has lower prevalence it could be imprecise; I would only act on it if the point estimate is clearly at or above the outcome_015 benchmark with an interval that excludes both null and clinically small effects. These are dataset-specific association tests, not causal or generalizable claims.

No assessments are due. I selected 12 previously registered but untested claims to maximize information about the strongest remaining near-threshold candidate and several robust main-effect screens. For all selected claims, direction is -1, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed level is associated with a more negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency, relative to the comparator. I am evaluating magnitude against approximate outcome-specific 10%-of-absolute-mean benchmarks: about 0.0301 for outcome_011, 0.0250 for outcome_015, 0.0269 for outcome_013, 0.0256 for outcome_016, and 0.0282 for outcome_008.

The first seven claims complete a focused feature_055 audit. H88 and H91 test level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_013 and outcome_011, directly extending the near-threshold H86 signal on outcome_015. H92 and H93 test level_002 versus level_001 and level_003 versus level_002 on outcome_015 to determine whether H86 reflects a robust level_003 association, an atypical level_001 baseline, or a level_003-versus-level_002 contrast. H94 and H95 test level_002 versus level_001 on outcome_013 and outcome_011, while H96 tests level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_008, giving cross-outcome consistency checks with reasonably large cells. This feature_055 block is now the most important evidence to accept, reject, defer, or later validate the family.

The remaining four claims are robust moderate-prevalence binary main-effect screens. H80 and H81 test feature_042 on outcome_015 and outcome_013, completing a cross-outcome screen where the prior outcome_006 contrast was imprecise. H82 and H83 test feature_065 on outcome_015 and outcome_016, extending the earlier outcome_008 screen and testing whether its upper-bound proximity to threshold has any correlated-outcome support. H90 tests feature_005 on outcome_015 as a new moderate-prevalence binary screen on the outcome with the lowest benchmark. I deferred H84, H85, H89, and H97 for now because feature_055 resolution and the feature_042/feature_065/feature_005 screens are more likely to produce decisive accept, reject, or defer decisions under the available 12-analysis budget. These remain dataset-specific association tests, not causal or generalizable conclusions.

All newly delivered comparisons are direction -1 mean differences, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed level is associated with a more negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency, relative to the comparator. I judged them against the 10%-of-absolute-mean benchmarks: about 0.0301 for outcome_011, 0.0250 for outcome_015, 0.0269 for outcome_013, 0.0256 for outcome_016, and 0.0282 for outcome_008. I did not formally multiplicity-adjust, but because many correlated screens have been run, I required a coherent threshold-level pattern rather than a marginal upper-bound crossing.

The feature_055 audit did not support a coherent level_003-versus-level_001 stronger-dependency signal. The original outcome_015 contrast H86 was only +0.0211 with an interval crossing zero, and the cross-outcome contrasts are weak or inconsistent: H88 on outcome_013 is +0.0059, H91 on outcome_011 is -0.0029, and H96 on outcome_008 is a statistically distinguishable opposite association, signed -0.0315 with CI -0.0611 to -0.0018. The level audit also fails to establish a clean ordering: H92 level_002-versus-level_001 on outcome_015 is +0.0069, H93 level_003-versus-level_002 is +0.0143, while H94 and H95 are near null or opposite. I therefore close the feature_055 positive-association family. H94 and H96 are rejected as clinically meaningful stronger-dependency associations; H94 has an upper bound below the outcome_013 benchmark, and H96 is significant in the opposite direction. The remaining ambiguous but low-priority feature_055 claims are unresolved and closed rather than treated as accepted. Because H96 itself suggests the raw direction may be clinically interesting as weaker dependency, I registered a reversed outcome_008 proposal with direction +1 for later evaluation, linked to H96 and motivated by R83.

The feature_042 cross-outcome screen is negative: H80 on outcome_015 and H81 on outcome_013 are centered near zero with confidence intervals entirely below the relevant clinical benchmark, so both are rejected and closed. H90, feature_005 on outcome_015, is not supported: the signed estimate is +0.0059, far below benchmark, with an interval compatible with null and only marginally above threshold; I defer it.

The most useful new candidate is H82, feature_065=1 versus 0 on outcome_015. It has a positive signed estimate of +0.0211 with a 95% interval from +0.0018 to +0.0404. This interval excludes the null and contains clinically meaningful values, but the point estimate is below the outcome_015 benchmark of about 0.0250 and the lower bound is clinically small. It is not acceptable on discovery alone. I request independent validation for H82 because it is the strongest remaining aligned near-threshold main effect with a positive interval, and independent evidence can decide whether it is a real threshold-level association or another multiplicity artifact. Cross-outcome feature_065 evidence is not encouraging: H83 on outcome_016 is opposite and below benchmark and is therefore rejected, while H8 on outcome_008 was not threshold-supported. H82 remains active pending validation.

From a critical-reviewer standpoint, the cell sizes are adequate, Welch comparisons are valid, and the sign convention was applied correctly. There is no evidence from this dataset that supports causal interpretation or generalizability, and all conclusions remain dataset-specific associations. The main multiplicity risk is high because these are many correlated outcome-by-predictor screens; therefore I accept no claim at this stage and use validation selectively only for H82.

No claim is accepted. The new validation for H82 resolves the strongest near-threshold feature_065 candidate. H82 is direction -1, so a positive signed estimate denotes a stronger-dependency association (more negative outcome_015) for feature_065=1 versus 0. The discovery estimate was +0.0211, just below the outcome_015 benchmark of about 0.0250, with interval +0.0018 to +0.0404. The independent validation estimate collapsed to +0.0044, with a multiplicity-adjusted interval of -0.0271 to +0.0359. This is close to null and includes negative differences; it fails to replicate the discovery signal. Because the claim was not threshold-supported on discovery, and independent evidence does not support even a positive point estimate, I reject H82 as not supported for a clinically meaningful stronger-dependency association. I close it. The feature_065 cross-outcome picture is also inconsistent: H83 on outcome_016 was rejected in the opposite direction, and H8 on outcome_008 remained unresolved without threshold support.

The current evidence base supports multiple dataset-specific negative findings. Broad screens for feature_034, feature_002, feature_060, feature_037, feature_054, feature_063, feature_055 positive family, feature_042, and feature_065 on several outcomes do not show clinically meaningful stronger-dependency associations once the 10%-of-absolute-mean threshold and uncertainty are considered. These are association findings in this supplied dataset only, not causal or generalizable claims.

The main remaining candidate is H98/H96: outcome_008 feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 in the reversed direction. With direction +1, the signed estimate is +0.0315, interval +0.0018 to +0.0611, against an outcome_008 benchmark of about 0.0282. This is statistically distinguishable from zero and the point estimate slightly exceeds the clinical threshold, but the lower confidence bound is far below threshold. Thus the dataset does not justify accepting the claim as clinically meaningful; uncertainty includes very small differences. It is nevertheless the most promising remaining threshold-level signal and should be audited and, if the audit supports it, considered for independent validation.

The next informative analyses are the new feature_055 level audits on outcome_008, together with the already active robust main-effect screens. I also registered feature_030/feature_064 screens on lower-benchmark outcomes outcome_006 and outcome_014, where the absolute-mean threshold is about 0.0093, because several existing near-null effects could become threshold-relevant if their point estimates remain stable. If feature_055 remains an isolated, unstable categorical result, it should be rejected rather than pursued further.

No assessments are currently due, and the accepted set remains empty. The highest-priority unresolved claim is H98: outcome_008 feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 with direction +1. With this sign convention, a positive estimate means the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is positive, i.e. the exposed level has a less negative dependency score and therefore weaker CRISPR dependency. The discovery signed estimate was +0.0315 with a 95% interval of +0.0018 to +0.0611, slightly above the outcome_008 benchmark of about 0.0282 but still too imprecise to accept because the lower bound is clinically tiny.

I register focused feature_055 audits. For direction +1 on outcome_008, the falsifiable question is whether the level_003-versus-level_001 association is part of a coherent categorical level pattern or an isolated contrast. The new level_004-versus-level_001 comparison tests whether another non-baseline level also differs from level_001. If feature_055 levels mark a real weaker-dependency state, level_004 should show a positive difference from level_001 and/or a near-null level_004-versus-level_003 difference. If level_004 is null, the original H98 signal is more likely level-specific or a multiplicity artifact. Existing active H99 and H100 will complete the level decomposition relative to level_001 and level_002.

I also register direct subgroup mean differences by feature_034 and feature_002 for the same level_003-versus-level_001 comparison. These are not validation tests; they test whether the raw association is coherent across major binary strata or is concentrated in one stratum. A plausible alternative explanation is confounding or effect heterogeneity: if the raw level_003-versus-level_001 difference is present in both feature_034 and feature_002 strata with comparable magnitude, it is less likely to be a simple artifact of subgroup composition. If it appears only in one stratum, the correct scientific claim should be narrowed to that subgroup or treated as exploratory. If the effect is opposite in a stratum, the overall association should be treated skeptically and probably closed unless validation resolves it.

For broader screening, I add three lower-priority comparisons: feature_030=1 versus 0 on low-benchmark outcome_014, feature_063 level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_013 as a cross-outcome check for the active outcome_015 H97 claim, and a first categorical screen of feature_048 level_002 versus the common level_003 on outcome_015. For direction -1, a positive signed estimate means the exposed group has a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency. Outcome_014 has a low benchmark of about 0.0093, so smaller raw differences can matter; however, these outcomes have wide uncertainty, so I will require a clear point estimate and interval behavior rather than accept a marginal upper-bound crossing. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

No assessments are due at this stage. The analysis request is prioritized toward the strongest unresolved candidate and a small set of high-information screens. The main candidate is the reversed feature_055 association on outcome_008: H98, feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 with direction +1. With this sign convention, a positive estimate means level_003 is associated with a less negative CRISPR dependency score than level_001, i.e. weaker dependency. Its discovery estimate was +0.0315, just above the approximate outcome_008 benchmark of 0.0282, but the confidence interval is wide and the lower bound is clinically small. I therefore request the remaining feature_055 level and stratum audits rather than accept it immediately.

The first seven analyses are intended to determine whether H98 is a coherent feature_055 pattern or an isolated contrast. H99 tests level_002 versus level_001, H100 tests level_003 versus level_002, and H104 tests level_004 versus level_001. If feature_055 levels mark a real weaker-dependency state relative to level_001, I would expect a broadly similar positive difference for nonbaseline levels, or at least a coherent pattern across level contrasts. H105 through H108 test the same level_003 versus level_001 association directly within feature_034 and feature_002 strata. If the effect appears only in one stratum, the claim should be narrowed or treated skeptically; if it is opposite in a stratum, the overall association is unlikely to be robust. If the level and stratum audits are inconsistent, I will probably close the reversed feature_055 family rather than spend validation.

The remaining five analyses are broad screens selected to preserve exploration while keeping the cell sizes large enough for Welch comparisons. H84 and H85 test feature_030=0 versus feature_030=1 and feature_064=0 versus feature_064=1 on outcome_015 with direction -1, so a positive estimate would mean the exposed group, the level-0 group, has stronger dependency. H101 and H102 test feature_030=1 versus feature_030=0 and feature_064=1 versus feature_064=0 on low-benchmark outcome_006 with direction -1, where a positive estimate means the presence of the exposure is associated with stronger dependency. Because outcome_006 has a low clinical benchmark of roughly 0.0093, smaller differences may matter, but its larger residual scale and correlated-screen multiplicity require a clear point estimate rather than marginal interval crossing. H111 is a first categorical screen of feature_048 on outcome_015, comparing less-common level_002 to the common level_003, also direction -1. These additional screens are dataset-specific association tests only and will not be interpreted causally or as generalizable.

For the outcome_008 feature_055 claims with direction +1, positive signed estimates mean the exposed level is associated with a less negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e. weaker dependency, relative to the comparator. The outcome_008 approximate 10%-of-absolute-mean benchmark is 0.0282. The feature_055 audit gives a mixed picture. H100 shows a positive signed estimate of +0.0321 with interval +0.0014 to +0.0628, supporting that level_003 differs from level_002 and is similar to the original H98 level_003-versus-level_001 signal. However, H99, level_002 versus level_001, is null (-0.0006), and H104, level_004 versus level_001, is slightly opposite (-0.0045) with an upper confidence limit of +0.0257 below benchmark. Thus the effect is not part of a broad nonbaseline-level pattern; it looks more like a level_003-specific contrast. H99 is closed unresolved because the point is null and the interval only barely reaches threshold; H104 is rejected because clinically meaningful positive values are excluded by the upper bound. The stratum audits show that H105 and H106 are positive but imprecise, so the association is not obviously confined to feature_034=1. In contrast, H107 is a much stronger candidate: within feature_002=1, the signed estimate is +0.0614, interval +0.0181 to +0.1047. The point is well above benchmark and the interval excludes the null, but the lower bound is below benchmark, so I do not accept it on discovery evidence. H108, the feature_002=0 complement, is essentially null (+0.0035). This suggests possible subgroup heterogeneity or concentration of the signal in feature_002=1, and it raises a multiple-comparisons concern because H107 was one of several stratum audits. H107 is nevertheless the strongest remaining threshold-level signal, so I request independent validation for H107 to determine whether this is a replicable subgroup-specific association or a multiplicity artifact. For the remaining new screens, H84 and H85 are rejected because their upper confidence bounds are below the outcome_015 benchmark and their points are not threshold-aligned. H101 is extremely imprecise around zero and is closed unresolved. H102 has a positive point estimate above the low outcome_006 benchmark but includes the null and is inconsistent with cross-outcome feature_064 evidence, so it is deferred unresolved. H111 is not supported because the exposed cell has only 25 observations, the point estimate is opposite to the hypothesized direction, and the interval is wide; it is closed unresolved. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

No claim is supported for acceptance at this stage. The new validation evidence resolves the main remaining candidate and also closes two earlier response/validation items. For H107, outcome_008 feature_055 level_003 versus level_001 within feature_002=1 with direction +1, a positive signed estimate denotes a weaker-dependency association, i.e. a less negative CRISPR dependency score. Discovery was strong: signed estimate +0.0614, 95% interval +0.0181 to +0.1047, above the outcome_008 benchmark of about 0.0282, but I withheld acceptance because the lower confidence bound was below benchmark and because the signal was selected among several correlated feature_055 audits. Independent validation failed: signed estimate -0.0124, multiplicity-adjusted interval -0.0650 to +0.0402. The validation point is opposite to the hypothesized weaker-dependency direction, and the interval is centered near null. Therefore H107 is rejected as not supported. This validation also substantially weakens the broader reversed feature_055 family. The overall H98 contrast was only marginally threshold-exceeding (+0.0315, interval +0.0018 to +0.0611); the strongest subgroup supporting it was H107, which failed, while H108 in the complement was null, H99 and H104 were null/opposite, H100 had a lower bound near null, and H105/H106 were imprecise. I therefore close H98, H100, H105, H106, and H108 as unresolved/closed rather than continue spending validation on an unstable categorical subgroup pattern. Closing as unresolved means the supplied dataset does not establish a clinically meaningful association; it does not prove a null effect.

H33, outcome_008 feature_060=1 versus 0 with direction -1, is also not supported. Discovery had a small positive signed estimate of +0.0064, interval -0.0151 to +0.0279. Validation was near null and opposite: signed estimate -0.0032, adjusted interval -0.0347 to +0.0283. The evidence is inconsistent and far below the outcome_008 benchmark, so H33 is rejected and closed. H48, outcome_016 feature_060-by-feature_002 interaction with direction -1, is likewise unsupported: discovery signed estimate +0.0070, interval -0.0247 to +0.0388; validation signed estimate -0.0046, adjusted interval -0.0515 to +0.0422. Discovery was imprecise, validation was opposite and null, so the interaction is rejected and closed. Across validated claims so far, the pattern is repeatedly failure of discovery near-threshold signals to replicate, which is exactly why I have accepted no claims.

The scientific picture is dominated by dataset-specific negative findings. Broad screens involving feature_034, feature_002, feature_060, feature_037, feature_054, feature_063, feature_055 positive/reversed contrasts, feature_042, feature_065, feature_030, feature_064, and several interactions have not produced a reproducible, threshold-supported association with CRISPR dependency outcomes. Biological interpretation remains uncertain because predictor labels are opaque, and these analyses are association summaries in the supplied dataset only, not causal or generalizable claims. The most informative next work is to move away from the failed feature_055 pattern and test whether earlier near-threshold binary predictors show coherent effects in low-benchmark outcomes. I registered follow-up screens for feature_027, feature_050, and feature_045 on outcome_006 and outcome_014, where the 10% benchmark is about 0.0093, together with the still-active existing screens for feature_037, feature_063 level_003, feature_064, and feature_030. If these low-benchmark screens do not yield a coherent, threshold-level pattern, further exploratory screening should be deprioritized in favor of concluding that the supplied evidence does not support any clinically meaningful predictor or subgroup association.
